edges.context: The formal deposition of Romulus Augustulus in 476 CE, marking the traditional end of the Western Roman Empire, occurred during Late Antiquity.
The construction of the Hagia Sophia (537 CE), a major architectural achievement of Late Antiquity, took place in Constantinople.
Emperor Justinian I (reigned 527-565 CE) was instrumental in the creation of the Codex Justinianus, a definitive legal compilation of Late Antiquity.
The Industrial Age represents a crucial sub-period within the broader Modern Era, spanning approximately 1760 CE to 1840 CE.
The intellectual and methodological advancements of the Scientific Revolution, culminating around the 18th century, profoundly influenced the technological innovations of the Industrial Age.
James Watt significantly improved the Newcomen steam engine in the 1760s, a pivotal invention that powered the Industrial Age.
The Industrial Age profoundly transformed Manchester, England, into a leading global center for textile production and industrial innovation during the late 18th and early 19th centuries.
The factory system and demand for labor during the Industrial Age directly caused unprecedented urbanization across Europe and North America from the late 18th century.
The Black Death (1346–1353) was a cataclysmic event that profoundly shaped the demographic, economic, and social landscape of the Late Medieval period.
The prolonged conflict between England and France (1337–1453) was a defining military and political feature of the Late Medieval era.
The technological innovation of the movable-type printing press by Johannes Gutenberg around 1440 emerged from and transformed the Late Medieval intellectual landscape.
The humanistic and artistic developments of the Late Medieval period, particularly in Italy, directly fostered the cultural explosion of the Renaissance.
The pivotal siege and capture of Constantinople by the Ottoman Empire in 1453 marked the end of the Byzantine Empire during the Late Medieval period.

The First Crusade (1096-1099) culminated in the capture of Jerusalem, establishing the Latin Kingdom and initiating a prolonged period of conflict in the Levant during the High Medieval period.
Thomas Aquinas's monumental Summa Theologica (completed c. 1274) synthesized Aristotelian philosophy with Christian theology, becoming a cornerstone of High Medieval scholastic thought.
The Magna Carta, signed in 1215 by King John of England, established precedents for constitutional law and limited monarchical power, profoundly influencing later developments of the rule of law.

edges.context: The disintegration of the Western Roman Empire in 476 CE is widely considered a primary catalyst for the beginning of the Medieval era in Europe.
The series of religious wars known as The Crusades occurred predominantly between 1096 CE and 1291 CE, entirely within the Medieval timeframe.
The devastating Black Death pandemic swept across Europe, Asia, and Africa between 1347 CE and 1351 CE, occurring during the late Medieval period.
Jerusalem served as a contested and religiously significant city throughout the Medieval era, particularly during the Crusades.
The intellectual and artistic developments of the late Medieval period directly influenced and set the stage for the subsequent Renaissance.
Renaissance Period is a sub-period within the broader Early Modern era
The intellectual and artistic flourishing of the Renaissance (c. 1300-1600 CE) laid the groundwork for the scientific and cultural shifts of the Early Modern era.
Gutenberg's printing press (c. 1440) dramatically accelerated the dissemination of knowledge and ideas, fostering the intellectual ferment of the Early Modern period.
Lisbon served as a crucial hub for Portuguese maritime expeditions and colonial ventures during the Age of Exploration in the 15th and 16th centuries.
The Scientific Revolution (c. 1543-1687) represents a fundamental shift in scientific thought and methodology that occurred entirely within the Early Modern period.

Adolf Hitler rose to power in Germany in 1933, consolidating dictatorial rule and initiating policies that profoundly shaped the latter half of the Interwar Period.
The unresolved political tensions, economic crises, and rise of aggressive totalitarian states during the Interwar Period directly caused the outbreak of World War II in 1939.
The extensive process of human evolution provides the biological and cultural context for the entire Prehistoric era, particularly from 70000 BCE.
The Neolithic Revolution, a transformative period of agricultural innovation, occurred within the later stages of the Prehistoric era from approximately 10,000 BCE.
The construction of the monumental site of Göbekli Tepe (c. 9500-8000 BCE) occurred in Anatolia during the Prehistoric Neolithic period.
The Prehistoric era witnessed the creation of sophisticated Paleolithic cave art, such as the famous paintings at Lascaux around 17,000 BCE.
Prehistoric agricultural and social developments in the Nile Valley directly influenced the emergence and structure of Ancient Egyptian Civilization from around 3100 BCE.
The harsh reparations and territorial losses imposed by the 1919 Treaty of Versailles significantly contributed to German resentment, a key factor leading to the World War II Era.
The World War II Era encompasses The Holocaust, the systematic, state-sponsored genocide of six million Jews by the Nazi regime and its collaborators from 1941 to 1945.
The pivotal Battle of Stalingrad, a turning point on the Eastern Front, occurred in the city of Stalingrad (now Volgograd), Russia, from August 1942 to February 1943.
The ideological and geopolitical power vacuum created by the World War II Era directly caused the onset of the Cold War between the United States and the Soviet Union.
The World War II Era profoundly transformed global geopolitics, dismantling old empires and establishing a new bipolar world order dominated by two superpowers.

The Korean War (1950-1953) was a major proxy conflict of the Cold War, fought on the Korean Peninsula with significant superpower involvement.
The United States was a principal antagonist in the Cold War, leading the Western Bloc and advocating for containment of communism.
The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 formally concluded the Cold War Era, dissolving one of its two primary belligerents.
